title: Celotex Corp. v. Catrett (1986)
summary: A defendant need not always produce affirmative evidence disproving the plaintiff’s claim; a supported showing of an absence of evidence may suffice.
notes:
The opinion quotes an earlier numbering of Rule 56. The casebook identifies the later numbering and discusses the 2010 changes. Do not describe the Supreme Court’s remand as a final finding that Catrett lacked evidence or that Celotex won the underlying case.

Justice Rehnquist wrote for a 5-4 Court (joined by White, Marshall, Powell and O'Connor); the opinion describes summary judgment as an integral part of the Federal Rules rather than a disfavored procedural shortcut, and Justice White's concurrence stressed that a movant cannot simply assert that the opponent has no evidence and must still support its motion.

sections.Parties: Myrtle Catrett sued asbestos companies, including Celotex, alleging that exposure to their products caused her husband’s death.
sections.Material Facts: Celotex relied on discovery responses that failed to identify witnesses connecting Louis Catrett to its asbestos products. Mrs. Catrett responded with three documents: her husband’s testimony in a compensation proceeding referring to a product called Firebar, a letter from an employer’s assistant secretary, and an insurer’s letter repeating information. The dispute concerned whether those materials supplied evidence of exposure and whether their substance could be presented in an admissible form.
sections.Procedural History: The district court granted summary judgment. The D.C. Circuit reversed because Celotex had not supplied affidavits or other evidence affirmatively disproving exposure. The Supreme Court reversed that legal rule and remanded the sufficiency and admissibility questions for consideration below. The casebook also describes the subsequent divided appellate ruling finding enough support to avoid summary judgment.
sections.Issue: Must a moving defendant submit affirmative evidence negating an essential element on which the plaintiff bears the trial burden?
sections.Holding: No. A properly supported identification of the absence of evidence can satisfy the movant’s initial responsibility, after which the plaintiff must identify specific facts supporting a genuine issue for trial.
sections.Reasoning: The majority linked Rule 56 to the burdens at trial. If the plaintiff cannot produce evidence of an essential element after an adequate opportunity for discovery, a trial cannot cure that evidentiary failure merely by repeating allegations. The movant still must inform the court of the motion’s basis and identify the relevant record; an unsupported assertion is not a substitute for the required showing. The Court read Adickes as consistent with this structure rather than as demanding affirmative negation in every case. It also emphasized protection against premature motions through the mechanism for obtaining necessary discovery. Because the court of appeals had not evaluated Mrs. Catrett’s actual materials, the Supreme Court left that task for remand.

learning.why: A defendant need not always produce affirmative evidence disproving the plaintiff’s claim; a supported showing of an absence of evidence may suffice.

topics.cp-summary-judgment: After adequate discovery, failure of proof on an essential element can support judgment without trial.
topics.cp-burden-production: A defendant may identify an absence of evidence on an element assigned to the plaintiff rather than submit affidavits negating it.
topics.cp-pleading-proof: The responding party must identify specific evidentiary facts rather than rely on the complaint.
topics.cp-procedure-merits: The Supreme Court remanded the adequacy of the plaintiff’s evidence rather than finally awarding judgment to Celotex.
topics.cp-judicial-discretion: The Celotex reading explains mandatory evidentiary requirements and the surrounding notes discuss the contested extent of discretion to deny an otherwise supported summary-judgment motion.
topics.cp-frcp-56: Celotex is the leading construction of the movant's burden under Rule 56.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice White emphasized that a conclusory assertion of no evidence was insufficient. Justice Brennan, joined by the Chief Justice and Justice Blackmun, agreed with the basic legal structure but believed Celotex had failed to address supporting material in the record. Justice Stevens also dissented; that opinion is omitted from the assigned excerpt.

mnemonic.rationale: Asbestos with no evidence of exposure
